status: Unverified survey candidates. Do not cite before independent primary-source checking.

works.fullAuthors: Sharif Noor Zisad, Ragib Hasan
works.title: LLMAC: A Global and Explainable Access Control Framework with Large Language Model
works.venue: in Proc. IEEE Consumer Commun. Netw. Conf. (CCNC), 2026, doi: 10.1109/CCNC65079.2026.11366514
works.contribution: Fine-tunes Mistral 7B on a synthetic policy dataset covering ownership verification, version management, workflow processes and dynamic role separation, so that a single LLM subsumes RBAC, ABAC and DAC. Reports 98.5% decision accuracy against RBAC 14.5%, ABAC 58.5% and DAC 27.5%, and emits a human-readable explanation alongside each allow/deny decision. Includes a response-time and resource-cost deployment study.
works.relevance: Closest published analogue to the SEBA-XAI decision core: an open-weight LLM fine-tuned to output an authorization decision plus a natural-language justification. It is the strongest baseline to cite and to distinguish from. Differences: LLMAC is a single trusted service with no ledger, no cryptographic binding of the attributes the model saw, and no independent re-execution — the explanation is free-form text that nothing verifies or commits. SEBA-XAI adds a deterministic policy engine re-executed by every endorsing peer that can override the model, an Ed25519 attestation tied to an on-chain adapter digest, an attribute hash that closes the TOCTOU window, and a structured explanation artifact (reason code, decisive attributes, counterfactual) hashed onto the ledger. LLMAC also has a binary allow/deny space, with no ESCALATE path to a human.

works.fullAuthors: Gelareh Hasel Mehri, Charles Morisset, Nicola Zannone
works.title: Towards Explainable Access Control [BlueSky Paper]
works.venue: in Proc. 30th ACM Symp. Access Control Models Technol. (SACMAT), 2025, doi: 10.1145/3734436.3734439
works.contribution: Defines the first formal model of access control explainability, framed as a quality measure over an explanation graph constructed around the decisions an AC system makes. Surveys existing access control literature to show how prior techniques can be recast as explanatory processes, and articulates three open challenges: collecting and interpreting AC decisions, constructing AC explanation graphs efficiently, and defining meaningful yet computationally tractable explanation-quality metrics. Explicitly notes the multi-stakeholder nature of AC (resource owners, administrators, end users), each needing different explanations.
works.relevance: The canonical framing paper for the explainability half of SEBA-XAI, and the right citation for 'what an access control explanation is and who it is for'. Its multi-stakeholder point maps directly onto the six-organisation setting, where a Police requester, an Authority department head adjudicating an escalation, and a Court auditor each need a different view of the same decision. It is a vision paper: it defines quality measures for explanations but does not build a system, does not use ML, and — the key gap SEBA-XAI fills — says nothing about the integrity of the explanation itself, i.e. how a stakeholder knows the explanation shown at audit time is the one that actually accompanied the decision.

works.fullAuthors: Gelareh Hasel Mehri, Clemens Dubslaff, Tim A. C. Willemse, Nicola Zannone
works.title: A Causal Framework for Explainable Access Control: [Work in Progress Paper]
works.venue: in Proc. 31st ACM Symp. Access Control Models Technol. (SACMAT), Waterloo, ON, Canada, 2026, doi: 10.1145/3750555.3811906
works.contribution: Introduces a causal framework that explains an authorization decision by identifying which policy elements are responsible for the outcome. Explanations are characterized through counterfactual reasoning and their influence quantified using principled measures of responsibility and blame, grounded in formal causality while permitting flexible abstraction over policy features so that explanations can be tailored to different analytical needs.
works.relevance: Provides the formal grounding for the two explanation components SEBA-XAI commits on-chain: decisive attributes correspond to its responsibility/blame measures, and the counterfactual corresponds directly to its counterfactual characterization. Best cited as the principled account of what a good access explanation should contain, against which SEBA-XAI's artifact schema can be justified. It is a work-in-progress theoretical paper operating over a deterministic policy: there is no learned model whose decision must be explained, no adversarial or integrity model, and no mechanism for recording explanations. SEBA-XAI must explain a neural decision that a deterministic engine can contradict, which is a case the causal framework does not cover.

works.fullAuthors: Shanampudi Pranaya Chowdary, Shamik Sural
works.title: EXTree: Towards Supporting Explainability in Attribute-based Access Control
works.venue: arXiv preprint arXiv:2604.12850, Apr. 2026
works.contribution: Represents ABAC policies as a tree jointly optimized for fast evaluation and human-centric feedback. Investigates two design dimensions: feedback evaluation strategies, i.e. how to craft actionable explanations when access is denied, and tree construction strategies, i.e. how to structure the policy tree for decisions that are both efficient and interpretable. Compares entropy-based, changeability-based and randomly generated trees across multiple configurations. Motivated explicitly by the observation that users expect more than silence when a request is denied.
works.relevance: The most direct prior work on the specific problem of explaining a DENY, and on making that explanation actionable rather than merely descriptive — the same goal as SEBA-XAI's counterfactual field. Its changeability-based construction is essentially a counterfactual-cost heuristic, which is a useful comparison point for how SEBA-XAI selects which attribute to name in a counterfactual. Differences: EXTree explains a deterministic tree it fully controls, so its explanation is a byproduct of policy structure and needs no verification. SEBA-XAI must explain a model decision whose internal logic is not a tree, must reconcile that with an independent deterministic engine, and must commit the explanation as a hashed audit artifact so it cannot be reconstructed differently after the fact.

works.fullAuthors: Lucía Cabanillas Rodríguez, Juan Manuel Montes-Lopez, Diego R. López, Pablo Serrano
works.title: DEBAC: Dynamic Explainable Behavior-Based Access Control
works.venue: in Proc. Joint Eur. Conf. Netw. Commun. & 6G Summit (EuCNC/6G Summit), 2025, doi: 10.1109/EuCNC/6GSummit63408.2025.11037037
works.contribution: Proposes a model-agnostic access control architecture in which Explainable Boosting Machines compute a real-time device trust score together with a human-interpretable explanation, and that explanation is passed to the policy decision point alongside the score so that the final access decision is itself explained. Comprises data collection, behavioral profiling, trust assessment and policy enforcement blocks. Validated on real campus WLAN traffic, reported at 94.3% accuracy and F1 of 0.95, with the stated aim of letting security teams see why access was granted or denied and refine policy accordingly.
works.relevance: The clearest prior instance of an ML model supplying both a decision input and its explanation to a policy decision point — architecturally the same seam SEBA-XAI sits on, with the model deliberately kept adjacent to rather than inside the enforcement path. Also the right citation for the argument that ML-based access control is unusable without explanation. Differences: DEBAC achieves explainability by choosing a glass-box model (EBM), whereas SEBA-XAI must extract explanations from an LLM; DEBAC has a single administrative domain and a single trusted decision point, no cross-organisational trust problem, no ledger, and no record binding the explanation to the decision — an operator of DEBAC's decision point could alter a logged explanation undetectably.

works.fullAuthors: Zhaohui Wang
works.title: Who Audits the Auditor? Tamper-Proof Fraud Detection with Blockchain-Anchored Explainable ML
works.venue: in Proc. IEEE Annu. Comput., Softw., Appl. Conf. (COMPSAC), SEPT Symp., 2026 (accepted); arXiv:2604.22096
works.contribution: Anchors both ML predictions and workflow execution to an immutable ledger, arguing that detection accuracy alone is insufficient when privileged operators can manipulate audit logs or bypass approval steps. Smart contracts enforce the approval workflow so that every transaction, prediction and explanation is atomically recorded and cannot be retroactively modified. Reports F1 = 0.895 and PR-AUC = 0.974, sub-25 ms inference latency, and under $0.01 per transaction on Layer-2, targeting GDPR Article 22 auditability.
works.relevance: The nearest work to SEBA-XAI's central integrity claim: it recognises that the explanation, not just the prediction, must be committed so a privileged insider cannot rewrite the justification after the fact, and it enforces the surrounding workflow in smart contracts rather than in application code. Cite it as the strongest statement of the threat model SEBA-XAI shares. Differences: it targets fraud detection rather than authorization, runs on a public Layer-2 chain rather than a permissioned consortium, and — critically — anchors the model output without binding it to the exact inputs the model saw or to an attested model identity. It has no attribute-hash TOCTOU defence, no adapter-digest attestation, and no deterministic re-execution that can override the model; the operator remains a single trusted party rather than a distinct MSP organisation signing its own transaction.

works.fullAuthors: S. Antony Joseph Raj, M. Madiajagan
works.title: TAE-IDS: a trust-aware explainable intrusion detection framework using attention-based meta-ensemble learning with blockchain validation
works.venue: Front. Artif. Intell., vol. 9, art. no. 1903112, 2026, doi: 10.3389/frai.2026.1903112
works.contribution: Combines a heterogeneous base-classifier ensemble (Logistic Regression, Extra Trees, XGBoost) whose uncertainty-aware meta-features (logits, confidence, entropy) feed a BiLSTM attention meta-classifier, with SHAP for global and local interpretation, and a SHA-256 tamper-evident validation layer for immutable intrusion logging and forensic verification of IDS outputs. Evaluated on UNSW-NB15 and CICIDS2017 in binary and multiclass settings. The paper is explicit that the validation layer is a lightweight custom Python hash chain on a single validation node, prioritising integrity preservation and forensic traceability over decentralised consensus.
works.relevance: A useful contrast case that names the exact shortcut SEBA-XAI avoids. It states the same goal — security decisions whose explanations are recorded so they can be verified forensically — but implements the ledger as a single-node hash chain, which yields tamper-evidence only against an attacker who does not control that node. In a six-organisation inter-agency setting the operator of the log is precisely the party an auditor must not have to trust, which is why SEBA-XAI commits to an endorsed Hyperledger Fabric transaction validated by peers of independent organisations. Also useful for its uncertainty-aware meta-features, a plausible signal for triggering ESCALATE, which TAE-IDS does not have (its outputs are attack classes, not authorization decisions with a human-in-the-loop path).

works.fullAuthors: Vinura Galwaduge, Jagath Samarabandu
works.title: Tabular Diffusion based Actionable Counterfactual Explanations for Network Intrusion Detection
works.venue: arXiv preprint arXiv:2507.17161, Jul. 2025
works.contribution: Argues that most XAI methods used in NIDS produce explanations that do not convert into actionable countermeasures, and proposes a diffusion-based counterfactual explanation framework for tabular network data. Presents what the authors state is the first comparative analysis of existing counterfactual explanation algorithms in the NIDS context, across three modern intrusion datasets, reporting more minimal and more diverse counterfactuals at lower generation time. Shows that instance-level counterfactuals can be summarized into global counterfactual rules that filter incoming attack queries at both instance and global level.
works.relevance: The methodological reference for counterfactual explanation in a security decision setting, and support for the design choice that SEBA-XAI's per-decision artifact carries a counterfactual rather than only a feature-attribution score — a denied officer needs to know what would have to change, not which feature had the largest weight. Its summarization of instance counterfactuals into global rules is a direct precedent for auditing accumulated on-chain explanations to recover an implied policy, which is a natural extension of SEBA-XAI's audit trail. Differences: it operates on continuous tabular traffic features with no notion of policy, identity or organisational trust; explanations are analyst-facing artifacts produced offline, not committed records that bind a decision, and nothing prevents them from being regenerated differently later.

works.fullAuthors: Gaith Rjoub, Jamal Bentahar, Omar Abdel Wahab, Rabeb Mizouni, Alyssa Song, Robin Cohen, Hadi Otrok, Azzam Mourad
works.title: A Survey on Explainable Artificial Intelligence for Cybersecurity
works.venue: IEEE Trans. Netw. Service Manage., vol. 20, no. 4, pp. 5115–5140, 2023, doi: 10.1109/TNSM.2023.3282740
works.contribution: Systematic survey of the state of the art in XAI for network cybersecurity, organized around a classification of network-driven threats and issues. Reviews the approaches proposed for making security models interpretable, and discusses the limitations of current XAI methods specifically in the cybersecurity context together with directions for future work. Highly cited (over 100 citations), and the standard reference for the black-box problem in security-critical AI.
works.relevance: The anchor citation establishing that XAI in security is a recognised field with an identified gap, and the natural opening reference for the Related Work subsection before narrowing to access control. Its central limitation — that surveyed XAI techniques treat the explanation as an analyst-facing output, evaluated for fidelity or plausibility but never for integrity, provenance or non-repudiation — is exactly the gap SEBA-XAI targets by making the explanation a signed, hashed, on-chain artifact produced by an organisationally distinct model operator. The survey also predates the use of LLMs as security decision-makers, so it does not address explaining a generative model's authorization decision.

works.fullAuthors: Haochen Sun, Jason Li, Hongyang Zhang
works.title: zkLLM: Zero Knowledge Proofs for Large Language Models
works.venue: in Proc. 2024 ACM SIGSAC Conf. Computer and Communications Security (CCS), 2024, pp. 4405-4419
works.contribution: Introduces the first zero-knowledge proof system specialised for LLM inference, contributing tlookup (a parallelised lookup argument for non-arithmetic tensor operations) and zkAttn (a ZKP tailored to the attention mechanism). On a CUDA implementation it produces a correctness proof of a full inference pass over a 13B-parameter model in under 15 minutes, with a proof under 200 kB that keeps model parameters private.
works.relevance: This is the strongest cryptographic answer to the question SEBA-XAI answers with attestation: how does a relying party know the LLM output it received was actually produced by the claimed model? Inference is executed off-chain and only the correctness proof is verifiable; the paper is a cryptographic construction and does not itself commit anything to a ledger. SEBA-XAI differs on cost and on trust model: it substitutes an Ed25519 attestation verified against a ledger-registered adapter digest, which is milliseconds rather than minutes and therefore usable in an interactive access-control loop, and it recovers the soundness zkLLM would have provided by re-executing a deterministic policy engine on every endorsing peer, so a forged or drifted model output is caught by disagreement rather than by a proof. zkLLM also proves nothing about the inputs' authenticity, whereas SEBA-XAI hashes the exact ledger-verified attributes the model saw.

works.fullAuthors: Bing-Jyue Chen, Suppakit Waiwitlikhit, Ion Stoica, Daniel Kang
works.title: ZKML: An Optimizing System for ML Inference in Zero-Knowledge Proofs
works.venue: in Proc. 19th European Conf. Computer Systems (EuroSys), 2024, pp. 560-574
works.contribution: Presents an optimising compiler from TensorFlow models to halo2 ZK-SNARK circuits, with hand-tuned gadgets for low-level operations and an optimiser that chooses circuit layouts; the authors report that layout choices alone change performance by up to 24x. It is the first framework to produce ZK-SNARKs for realistic models including state-of-the-art vision models, a distilled GPT-2, and the model behind Twitter's recommendation feed.
works.relevance: ZKML frames the motivating tension precisely as SEBA-XAI does — decisions are made behind a closed system, transparency is demanded, but the operator has legitimate reasons (privacy, trade secrets) not to release weights — and resolves it by proving the computation rather than disclosing the model. Execution remains off-chain; the SNARK is what a verifier (possibly a smart contract) checks. SEBA-XAI resolves the same tension organisationally instead of cryptographically: the model operator is a distinct MSP organisation whose signed decision is a separate on-chain transaction, so accountability comes from a named, sanctionable signer plus deterministic re-execution, not from a circuit. This is what makes a 14B decoder-only model tractable, which is well outside what ZKML's circuits accommodate.

works.fullAuthors: KD Conway, Cathie So, Xiaohang Yu, Kartin Wong
works.title: opML: Optimistic Machine Learning on Blockchain
works.venue: arXiv preprint arXiv:2401.17555, 2024
works.contribution: Proposes optimistic ML inference for blockchains: a submitter posts a result which is accepted unless challenged, and disputes are resolved by an interactive fraud-proof protocol in the style of optimistic rollups, using a multi-phase protocol with semi-native execution and lazy loading. The design lets a 7B-LLaMA model be run on a commodity PC without a GPU, at far lower cost than zkML.
works.relevance: opML is the principal non-cryptographic alternative for getting LLM-scale inference into a blockchain's trust boundary, and it is the closest competitor to SEBA-XAI's attestation approach in cost profile. Crucially, inference is never executed on-chain and nothing is proven on-chain in the common case — the chain only arbitrates a single disputed instruction step during a challenge, and finality is delayed by a challenge window. That delay is unacceptable for an interactive access-control decision on a criminal case record, so SEBA-XAI achieves immediate finality instead: the deterministic policy engine re-executed by every endorsing peer adjudicates the model's output within the same transaction, and any disagreement becomes a human escalation rather than a post-hoc fraud proof.

works.fullAuthors: Zhikai Li, Steve Vott, Bhaskar Krishnamachari
works.title: ML2SC: Deploying Machine Learning Models as Smart Contracts on the Blockchain
works.venue: in Proc. IEEE Int. Conf. Blockchain and Cryptocurrency (ICBC), 2024, pp. 645-649
works.contribution: Builds a PyTorch-to-Solidity translator that automatically emits a smart-contract implementation of a multi-layer perceptron, approximating floating-point arithmetic with a fixed-point library; weights trained off-chain are transferred to the contract by a function call and inference is then invoked on-chain. The authors model gas cost analytically, show it grows linearly in MLP size, and verify that on-chain outputs are identical to the off-chain PyTorch originals.
works.relevance: This is the reference point for genuinely on-chain inference — the model is executed by the consensus protocol itself, which is the strongest possible integrity guarantee and exactly what SEBA-XAI cannot do. ML2SC also delimits why: gas cost scales linearly with parameter count for an MLP, so a 14B-parameter decoder-only transformer is many orders of magnitude beyond feasible, and a fixed-point Solidity reimplementation of attention would not be bit-reproducible across peers in any case. SEBA-XAI therefore keeps the LLM off-chain and puts only a deterministic, cheaply re-executable policy engine in chaincode, which recovers ML2SC's every-peer-agrees property for the part of the decision that must be authoritative.

works.fullAuthors: Ke Wang, Zishuo Zhao, Xinyuan Song, Zelin Li, Libin Xia, Chris Tong, Bill Shi, Wenjie Qu, Eric Yang, Lynn Ai
works.title: VeriLLM: A Lightweight Framework for Publicly Verifiable Decentralized Inference
works.venue: arXiv preprint arXiv:2509.24257, 2025
works.contribution: Proposes a publicly verifiable protocol for decentralised LLM serving in which verifiers re-run inference selectively at roughly 1% of the underlying cost by exploiting the structural separation between prefill and autoregressive decoding, backed by minimal on-chain checks that preclude free-riding. It introduces an isomorphic inference-verification architecture that multiplexes both roles onto the same GPU workers and enforces task indistinguishability so nodes cannot behave selectively.
works.relevance: VeriLLM is the current best statement of verification-by-replication for LLM inference and is precise about the division of labour SEBA-XAI must also make explicit: the model runs off-chain, replication establishes correctness, and the chain carries only lightweight checks and the economic hooks. Its threat model is a permissionless one with untrusted, financially motivated workers and no trusted nodes. SEBA-XAI's setting inverts that assumption — the operator is a known, permissioned MSP organisation subject to governance rather than an anonymous worker — so replication and incentive engineering are unnecessary, and integrity comes instead from a signed attestation bound to a registered adapter digest plus deterministic policy re-execution. VeriLLM also verifies only that some output is faithful to the model, not that the inputs were the authentic ledger state, which is the TOCTOU gap SEBA-XAI closes with an attribute hash.

works.fullAuthors: Zhenjie Zhang, Yuyang Rao, Hao Xiao, Xiaokui Xiao, Yin Yang
works.title: Proof of Quality: A Costless Paradigm for Trustless Generative AI Model Inference on Blockchains
works.venue: arXiv preprint arXiv:2405.17934, 2024
works.contribution: Proposes proof of quality (PoQ), which abandons validation of the inference procedure altogether and instead has validators score the quality of the produced output using lightweight BERT-based cross-encoders. The realisation, PQML, targets open-source generative models such as Llama 3 and Mixtral; quality checks complete within a second on CPU alone and consensus is reached in milliseconds.
works.relevance: PoQ is the third distinct answer in this design space, alongside proving (zkLLM, ZKML) and replicating (opML, VeriLLM): validate the outcome, not the computation. It is the right contrast for explaining why SEBA-XAI does not adopt outcome scoring. An access-control verdict is a three-way categorical label, not free text, so a learned quality score is both unnecessary and unsound as an authority — a plausible-looking ALLOW that violates a statutory rule would score well. SEBA-XAI replaces the learned judge with a deterministic policy engine that every endorsing peer re-executes and that overrides the model outright, converting the equivalent of a low-quality output into a mandatory human escalation rather than a probabilistic rejection.

works.fullAuthors: Fan Zhang, Ethan Cecchetti, Kyle Croman, Ari Juels, Elaine Shi
works.title: Town Crier: An Authenticated Data Feed for Smart Contracts
works.venue: in Proc. 2016 ACM SIGSAC Conf. Computer and Communications Security (CCS), 2016, pp. 270-282
works.contribution: Presents an authenticated data feed that bridges smart contracts and existing HTTPS websites by pairing a blockchain front end with an Intel SGX trusted-hardware back end that scrapes sources and serves source-authenticated data to relying contracts, with support for encrypted request parameters and access-controlled sources. The system is formally modelled and its security properties proved in the Universal Composability framework, with an Ethereum implementation and gas and TCB analyses.
works.relevance: Town Crier is the origin of the attestation pattern SEBA-XAI generalises: an off-chain computation the chain cannot perform is executed in an environment whose identity the chain can verify, and its output enters the ledger as authenticated data rather than as a proof or a replicated computation. It also establishes the security question SEBA-XAI must answer — an attested feed is only as trustworthy as the binding between the attestation and the exact request it answers. SEBA-XAI carries no ML and no TEE here; it substitutes an Ed25519 key whose adapter digest is registered on the ledger for hardware attestation, and it strengthens the binding by hashing both the query and the precise ledger-verified attribute snapshot the model consumed, so a replayed or stale attestation fails validation.

works.fullAuthors: Marco Esposito, Francesco Bruschi, Donatella Sciuto
works.title: Cognitive oracles: On-chain explainable machine learning
works.venue: Computer Communications, vol. 251, art. 108467, Apr. 2026
works.contribution: Proposes a cognitive oracle that makes complex, ambiguous predicates (for example, identifying specific elements within an image) verifiable on-chain by pairing ML classifiers with SNARK proofs, going beyond the scalar data feeds of conventional oracles. To absorb classifier error it embeds a jury-based dispute-resolution layer supported by verifiable ML explanations, evaluated on a carbon-credit application over small neural networks; the authors find viability depends on keeping dispute frequency low, and that adding explanations increases game-theoretic complexity but improves jury decisions, transparency and trust. An earlier conference version appeared as M. Esposito, F. Bruschi, M. Montecalvo and D. Sciuto, 'Cognitive Oracles: Provable on-chain assessment through Validity Machine Learning,' in Proc. IEEE PerCom Workshops, 2024, pp. 537-542.
works.relevance: This is the closest work to SEBA-XAI on the explainability axis and the only one in this group that treats a machine-produced explanation as a first-class on-chain artifact rather than a UI nicety, and that routes contested ML judgements to human adjudicators. Its architecture is proof-based — the classifier runs off-chain and a SNARK is verified on-chain — and it works over small networks on a public chain, with explanations serving as evidence for a jury of economically incentivised, anonymous participants. SEBA-XAI mirrors the structure at LLM scale and in a permissioned setting: explanations are reason codes, decisive attributes and a counterfactual, hashed and committed as an audit artifact rather than proved in a circuit, and the human escalation path is triggered deterministically when the policy engine and the model disagree, not by a staked challenge whose frequency governs economic viability.

works.fullAuthors: Mahdi Manavi, Yunpeng Zhang, Guoning Chen
works.title: Smart Blockchain-Based Access Control for the Internet of Things
works.venue: in Proc. 35th Int. Conf. Computer Communications and Networks (ICCCN), 2026
works.contribution: Proposes a risk-adaptive enforcement layer for Hyperledger Fabric that couples an off-chain LSTM risk oracle with deterministic on-chain checks: the oracle assigns each request to a Low, Moderate or High tier and issues a signed attestation bound to the client identity and the target key and version, which endorsing peers verify in chaincode before enforcing a tier-conditioned state-based endorsement policy, without modifying the ordering service or consensus. Testbed experiments show stricter validation for higher-risk requests while benign traffic retains near-baseline confirmation latency.
works.relevance: This is the nearest prior work to SEBA-XAI overall and must be distinguished carefully: it is the same platform (Hyperledger Fabric), the same architectural move (off-chain neural model, signed attestation verified deterministically in chaincode), and even the same defence against stale inputs (binding the attestation to the target key and version, analogous to the attribute hash). The differences are the contribution claims. First, its model is an LSTM emitting a coarse risk tier from request telemetry, whereas SEBA-XAI's fine-tuned Qwen3-14B consumes a natural-language request plus ledger-verified attributes and emits the access verdict itself. Second, the attested tier is trusted and merely parameterises the endorsement policy, whereas in SEBA-XAI a deterministic policy engine re-executed by every peer overrides the model and forces human escalation on disagreement. Third, it produces no explanation artifact. Fourth, the oracle is an external service, not a first-class MSP organisation, so the request and the decision are not two transactions signed by two mutually accountable parties. Fifth, the setting is IoT device access rather than multi-agency criminal case records with statutory disclosure constraints.

works.fullAuthors: Mahdi Manavi, Yunpeng Zhang, Guoning Chen
works.title: Smart Blockchain-Based Access Control for the Internet of Things
works.venue: in Proc. 35th Int. Conf. Comput. Commun. Netw. (ICCCN), 2026
works.contribution: Adds a risk-adaptive enforcement layer to Hyperledger Fabric: an off-chain LSTM risk oracle ingests request metadata (operation, key/namespace, client identity, temporal and behavioural features) plus historical trust state and assigns each request a Low/Moderate/High tier, then issues a signed attestation bound to the client identity and the target key/version. Endorsing peers verify that attestation inside chaincode and apply tier-conditioned state-based endorsement policies, leaving the ordering service and consensus untouched. A Fabric testbed shows stricter endorsement for high-risk requests with near-baseline confirmation latency for normal traffic.
works.relevance: This is the closest architectural analogue to SEBA-XAI and must anchor the Related Work: it establishes the same off-chain-inference / on-chain-verification pattern on Fabric, with a signed attestation bound to the target key and version to prevent substitution. SEBA-XAI differs on three axes. (i) Model class and output: an LSTM emitting a coarse three-tier risk label versus a fine-tuned Qwen3-14B reasoning over a natural-language request and ledger-verified attributes to emit a full ALLOW/DENY/ESCALATE authorisation decision. (ii) Governance of the model: Manavi et al. treat the oracle as trusted infrastructure outside the membership structure, whereas SEBA-XAI makes the model operator a first-class MSP organisation (AIOrgMSP) with its own peer, so request and decision are two transactions signed by two distinct parties, and the Ed25519 attestation is checked against an adapter digest registered on the ledger. (iii) Adjudication and explanation: their scheme has no deterministic re-execution that can overrule the oracle and no explanation artifact, while SEBA-XAI re-executes a deterministic policy engine on every endorsing peer, converts any model/engine disagreement into a human escalation, and commits a reason code, decisive attributes and a counterfactual as hashed audit evidence.

works.fullAuthors: Sharif Noor Zisad, Ragib Hasan
works.title: LLMAC: A Global and Explainable Access Control Framework with Large Language Model
works.venue: in Proc. IEEE Consum. Commun. Netw. Conf. (CCNC), 2026
works.contribution: Fine-tunes Mistral 7B as a single unified access-control decision engine that subsumes RBAC, ABAC and DAC, trained on a synthetic dataset covering ownership verification, version management, workflow processes and dynamic separation of duty. Reports 98.5% decision accuracy against RBAC (14.5%), ABAC (58.5%) and DAC (27.5%) baselines on that dataset, emits a human-readable explanation with each decision, and includes a latency and resource study arguing for practical deployment.
works.relevance: The single most direct precedent for SEBA-XAI's core claim that a parameter-efficient fine-tuned mid-size open-weight LLM can act as the policy decision point rather than merely as a policy authoring aid, and that it can carry a natural-language justification. It is the right paper to position against because it shares the model scale (7B versus 14B-4bit), the fine-tuning strategy, and the explainability ambition. The differences define SEBA-XAI's contribution: LLMAC is a centralised, single-trust-domain service with no ledger, so nothing binds the decision to the exact attribute state it was computed from, nothing prevents a compromised or silently swapped model from producing decisions that verify, and its free-text explanation is not committed anywhere and cannot be audited after the fact. SEBA-XAI hashes the attributes the model saw (closing the TOCTOU window), hashes the query, verifies an Ed25519 attestation against a ledger-registered adapter digest, and commits a structured reason code, decisive attributes and counterfactual as an on-chain audit artifact across six organisations. LLMAC also has no deterministic fallback: its 1.5% error rate is unadjudicated, whereas in SEBA-XAI a policy-engine disagreement forces escalation to a human.

works.fullAuthors: Mohammad Nur Nobi, Ram Krishnan, Yufei Huang, Mehrnoosh Shakarami, Ravi Sandhu
works.title: Toward Deep Learning Based Access Control
works.venue: in Proc. 12th ACM Conf. Data Appl. Secur. Privacy (CODASPY), Baltimore, MD, USA, 2022, pp. 143-154, doi: 10.1145/3508398.3511497
works.contribution: Proposes DLBAC, which replaces the hand-engineered access-control model with a learned neural network that maps subject and object metadata directly to an access decision, arguing this removes the burden of engineering an abstract policy model. Evaluates a candidate architecture, DLBAC_alpha, on real-world and synthetic datasets and addresses accuracy, generalisation to unseen subjects/objects, and explainability of individual decisions via feature-attribution and knowledge-transfer techniques.
works.relevance: The foundational, heavily cited statement of the position SEBA-XAI adopts and extends: that a neural network can serve as the decision function itself, not just as a tool that drafts rules for a conventional engine, and that such a decision function must be explainable to be deployable. It supplies the standard framing for the accuracy/generalisation/explainability triad and the standard critique that learned deciders are opaque. SEBA-XAI departs from DLBAC in three ways. DLBAC consumes structured metadata vectors, while SEBA-XAI consumes an unstructured natural-language request alongside ledger-verified attributes, which is the operationally realistic form of an inter-agency records request. DLBAC produces a binary permit/deny, while SEBA-XAI produces a three-valued ALLOW/DENY/ESCALATE that routes residual uncertainty to a human head of department in the Authority organisation. Most importantly, DLBAC assumes a single trusted enforcement point; SEBA-XAI places the decider inside a six-organisation permissioned Fabric network where the decision is attested, hashed and endorsed by peers that independently re-execute a deterministic policy engine, so no single party can assert a decision unilaterally.

works.fullAuthors: Charles Fleming, Ashish Kundu, Ramana Kompella
works.title: Uncertainty-Aware, Risk-Adaptive Access Control for Agentic Systems using an LLM-Judged TBAC Model
works.venue: arXiv preprint arXiv:2510.11414, 2025
works.contribution: Extends Task-Based Access Control by using an LLM as an autonomous risk-aware judge for novel tasks that no predefined policy covers. On receiving a proposed task the LLM synthesises a just-in-time policy while simultaneously computing a composite risk score for the target resource and an estimate of its own model uncertainty; high-risk or high-uncertainty requests trigger stricter controls, including mandatory human approval, giving an adaptive enforcement of least privilege.
works.relevance: This is the clearest existing justification for a three-valued decision space rather than a binary one: it establishes routing to human approval as the principled response to model uncertainty or elevated resource risk, which is exactly the role of SEBA-XAI's ESCALATE label and its escalation to department heads in the Authority organisation. Citing it lets SEBA-XAI ground ESCALATE in prior art rather than presenting it as an ad hoc third class. The contrast is that Fleming et al. derive the escalation trigger from the model's own self-reported confidence, so the model is judge of both the decision and of when it should be overruled, and the framework is a single-domain enterprise service with no cryptographic record of what was decided. SEBA-XAI externalises the trigger: a deterministic policy engine re-executed by every endorsing peer overrides the model, and any model/engine disagreement mechanically becomes an escalation, so the decision to defer to a human does not depend on the model's introspection. SEBA-XAI additionally binds each decision to a hash of the attributes and the query and commits it on-chain, which a self-judging LLM service cannot offer.

works.fullAuthors: Friederike Groschupp, Daniele Lain, Aritra Dhar, Lara Magdalena Lazier, Srdjan Capkun
works.title: Can LLMs Make (Personalized) Access Control Decisions?
works.venue: arXiv preprint arXiv:2511.20284, 2025 (rev. 2026)
works.contribution: Empirically measures how well LLMs can act as runtime access-control deciders aligned to a user's stated security preferences. Using smartphone permission requests as the case study, the authors collect 307 natural-language user privacy statements and 14,682 corresponding human permission decisions, then compare a general LLM decider against a personalised one that conditions on the user's stated preferences, with user feedback gathered on 1,298 of the personalised decisions. LLMs agree with the majority human decision in up to 86% of cases and can nudge users toward safer choices, but personalisation exposes a trade-off: closer adherence to individual preferences yields less safe outcomes because users over-permission.
works.relevance: The strongest empirical evidence available for the premise SEBA-XAI is built on and for the safeguard it adds. It confirms that an LLM reasoning over request context can approximate a correct authorisation decision at useful rates, which legitimises the model as a decision component; and it quantifies the residual disagreement, showing that even at 86% agreement an LLM decider left unchecked is not acceptable where the resource is criminal case evidence. This is precisely the argument for SEBA-XAI's deterministic policy engine, re-executed by every endorsing peer, holding override authority over the model, and for converting disagreement into human escalation rather than silently accepting the model's output. The setting also differs in a way worth stating: their deciders are personalised to individual consumer preferences on a single device, whereas SEBA-XAI decides against organisational policy that is agreed across six agencies, registered on-chain, and identical for every endorser, so correctness is defined by a shared committed policy rather than by an individual's taste.

works.fullAuthors: Luca Petrillo, Fabio Martinelli, Antonella Santone, Francesco Mercaldo
works.title: Explainable Access Control Policies Classification through Large Language Models
works.venue: in Proc. Int. Joint Conf. Neural Netw. (IJCNN), 2025, pp. 1-9, doi: 10.1109/IJCNN64981.2025.11228393
works.contribution: Fine-tunes four language-model architectures (BERT, GPT-Neo, RoBERTa, XLNet) to classify access-control policy text from a labelled corpus of 1,522 samples, comparing full fine-tuning against parameter-efficient fine-tuning as a performance/efficiency trade-off. Best configuration reaches 0.91 accuracy and 0.93 F1 (0.97 precision, 0.90 recall), and integrated gradients are applied to the best model to attribute predictions back to input tokens, making the classifier's behaviour inspectable.
works.relevance: Directly supports two of SEBA-XAI's methodological choices with peer-reviewed IEEE evidence: that parameter-efficient fine-tuning (LoRA in SEBA-XAI's case, PEFT here) is the right adaptation strategy for access-control language tasks, and that a fine-tuned transformer's access-control output should be paired with an attribution-based explanation rather than shipped as a bare label. The gap it leaves is the one SEBA-XAI closes. Their task is offline classification of policy text, not runtime authorisation of a live request against current subject and resource state, so there is no notion of attribute freshness, no enforcement point and no adversary. Their explanation is a post-hoc token-attribution map produced by the same party that produced the prediction, held locally and never bound to anything; SEBA-XAI instead emits a structured, human-legible explanation (reason code, decisive attributes, counterfactual), hashes it, and commits it as an audit artifact on a ledger shared by six organisations, so the justification is independently verifiable and non-repudiable rather than merely available.

works.fullAuthors: Thang Bui, Esteban Martinez Mota
works.title: Mining Attribute-Based Access Control Policies with Large Language Models [Work in Progress Paper]
works.venue: in Proc. 31st ACM Symp. Access Control Models Technol. (SACMAT), 2026, pp. 45-51, doi: 10.1145/3750555.3811907
works.contribution: Presents what the authors describe as the first systematic zero-shot evaluation of LLMs as ABAC policy miners. A prompting framework supplies complete attribute data and the granted permissions derived from ground-truth ABAC policies and constrains the model's output to valid ABAC structures; generated policies are scored by semantic similarity to the original permission set and syntactic similarity to the reference rules. LLMs produce concise, meaningful rules that track ground truth on small datasets but degrade on larger ones and frequently emit over-permissive rules; the authors flag automated validation and natural-language explanations as needed future work.
works.relevance: Represents the dominant alternative use of LLMs in access control, which SEBA-XAI deliberately does not adopt: the LLM writes the policy offline and a conventional engine then enforces it, so the model never touches a live request. Contrasting with it sharpens SEBA-XAI's positioning as a policy decision point rather than a policy authoring tool, and its finding that zero-shot LLMs systematically over-permit and degrade with scale is the direct empirical case against trusting an unconstrained LLM's authorisation output, motivating both SEBA-XAI's task-specific LoRA fine-tuning over zero-shot prompting and its deterministic override. Their own stated future work, automated validation to suppress over-permissions and natural-language explanations for interpretability, describes almost exactly what SEBA-XAI implements, but SEBA-XAI implements it as consensus-enforced re-execution across six organisations' endorsing peers and as a hashed on-chain explanation artifact, not as a post-processing step under the model operator's control.

works.fullAuthors: Sakuna Harinda Jayasundara, Nalin Asanka Gamagedara Arachchilage, Giovanni Russello
works.title: SoK: Access Control Policy Generation from High-level Natural Language Requirements
works.contribution: A systematic literature review of 49 publications on turning high-level natural-language requirements into access-control policies, covering both graphical policy configuration tools and automated policy generation frameworks. The authors argue administrator-centred access-control failures drive data breaches, and characterise the two failure modes of existing solutions: graphical configuration tools are error-prone and therefore unusable at scale, while automated generation frameworks make erroneous predictions and are therefore unreliable. The review catalogues these limitations as design requirements for future systems.
works.relevance: The standard survey anchor for the natural-language-to-policy line of work and the cleanest citation for the usability-versus-reliability dilemma that motivates SEBA-XAI's hybrid design. Its central finding, that automated generation is unreliable because predictions are erroneous and nothing catches the errors, is the literature-level justification for pairing the learned decider with a deterministic policy engine re-executed by every endorsing peer and escalating disagreements to a human, rather than trusting either a hand-configured policy or a model prediction alone. It also lets the Related Work establish the scoping distinction SEBA-XAI depends on: the surveyed body of work generates policy artifacts from requirements documents ahead of time, whereas SEBA-XAI evaluates an individual live request at runtime against ledger-verified attributes and commits the outcome, an enforcement-time problem the survey does not cover, and none of the surveyed systems addresses multi-organisation trust, attestation of the deciding component, or non-repudiable audit.

works.fullAuthors: Ye Cheng, Minghui Xu, Yue Zhang, Kun Li, Hao Wu, Yechao Zhang, Shaoyong Guo, Wangjie Qiu, Dongxiao Yu, Xiuzhen Cheng
works.title: Say What You Mean: Natural Language Access Control with Large Language Models for Internet of Things
works.venue: arXiv preprint arXiv:2505.23835, 2025
works.contribution: Presents LACE, a hybrid Language-based Access Control Engine that combines prompt-guided policy generation, retrieval-augmented reasoning and formal validation. Users state policies in natural language; LACE translates them into structured rules, validates their semantic correctness, and then makes runtime access decisions through a hybrid LLM-plus-rule-based engine. Evaluated in smart-home settings, it reports 100% correctness on verified policy generation and up to 88% decision accuracy with 0.79 F1 using DeepSeek-V3, beating GPT-3.5 and Gemini baselines, and scales under increasing policy volume and request concurrency.
works.relevance: The closest non-blockchain precedent for SEBA-XAI's central design pattern: a hybrid decision path in which an LLM's output is constrained by a deterministic rule engine and a formal validation step, yielding decisions the authors characterise as interpretable and verifiable. It confirms that the hybrid arrangement outperforms both rigid rule matching and an unconstrained LLM, which is the same argument SEBA-XAI makes for its policy engine. The differences are what SEBA-XAI contributes. LACE's validation and its rule engine execute in one trust domain on the same host as the model, so 'verifiable' means internally checked, not independently checkable by a relying party; SEBA-XAI's deterministic engine is re-executed by every endorsing peer across six organisations, and disagreement between engine and model is not silently resolved but escalated to a human. LACE also has no adversary model for the model itself: nothing attests which model weights produced a decision, nothing pins the attribute snapshot the decision was computed over, and no record survives the request. SEBA-XAI supplies all three via the ledger-registered adapter digest, the attribute and query hashes, and the committed explanation artifact, and its domain is inter-agency criminal case records rather than smart-home devices, where non-repudiation is a legal requirement rather than a convenience.

works.fullAuthors: Han Liu, Dezhi Han, Dun Li
works.title: Fabric-iot: A Blockchain-Based Access Control System in IoT
works.venue: IEEE Access, vol. 8, pp. 18207-18218, 2020
works.contribution: Builds an ABAC system on Hyperledger Fabric out of three chaincodes: a Device Contract storing resource URLs, a Policy Contract that lets admin users manage ABAC policies, and an Access Contract that performs the access decision for normal users. Evaluated with two simulation experiment groups measuring throughput and consensus behaviour under large-scale request load.
works.relevance: This is the canonical Fabric-plus-ABAC baseline and the closest structural analogue to SEBA-XAI's chaincode layer: policies as ledger state, decisions as chaincode execution. It differs in that the decision function is a fixed rule evaluation written by hand into the Access Contract, with no learned component, no natural-language request, and no reason code, decisive attributes or counterfactual emitted with the decision. It also has no notion of a model-operator organisation; every organisation is a data producer or consumer, so there is no second signing party for the decision itself.

works.fullAuthors: Yuanyu Zhang, Shoji Kasahara, Yulong Shen, Xiaohong Jiang, Jianxiong Wan
works.title: Smart Contract-Based Access Control for the Internet of Things
works.venue: IEEE Internet of Things Journal, vol. 6, no. 2, pp. 1594-1605, Apr. 2019
works.contribution: Proposes a framework of multiple Access Control Contracts (one per subject-object pair), a single Judge Contract and a single Register Contract. Each ACC does static validation against predefined policies plus dynamic validation of subject behaviour; the JC receives misbehaviour reports from the ACCs, judges them and returns a penalty; the RC registers and manages the methods and their contracts. Demonstrated on Ethereum with a desktop, a laptop and two Raspberry Pis.
works.relevance: The most-cited smart-contract access control design and the standard reference for the claim that authorisation logic can live entirely in deterministic on-chain code. Its dynamic validation is behaviour-based penalty accounting, not learned inference over request semantics. SEBA-XAI keeps a deterministic engine of exactly this kind but demotes it to an override channel that adjudicates against an off-chain model, and its escalation path routes disagreement to a human rather than to an automated judging contract. Zhang et al. also run on permissionless Ethereum, so requester and decision-maker are not distinct MSP organisations.

works.fullAuthors: Ronghua Xu, Yu Chen, Erik Blasch, Genshe Chen
works.title: BlendCAC: A BLockchain-Enabled Decentralized Capability-Based Access Control for IoTs
works.venue: Proc. 2018 IEEE Int. Conf. Internet of Things (iThings) / GreenCom / CPSCom / SmartData, pp. 1027-1034, 2018
works.contribution: Introduces a decentralized capability-based access control mechanism in which a federated capability delegation model supports hierarchical, multi-hop delegation, and an identity-based capability token management strategy uses smart contracts for registration, propagation and revocation of authorization. Implemented on a Raspberry Pi and a local private blockchain network. An extended journal version appeared in Computers, vol. 7, no. 3, art. 39, 2018.
works.relevance: Represents the capability-token branch of blockchain access control, where the ledger holds transferable authorisations rather than evaluating a policy per request. It is the relevant contrast for SEBA-XAI's decision that is minted per request and bound to a specific attribute snapshot: a capability token, once issued, is valid until revoked and carries no record of the attribute state that justified it, which is precisely the TOCTOU exposure SEBA-XAI closes with an on-chain hash of the attributes the model saw. Delegation is also human-configured here, with no inference and no reason artifact.

works.fullAuthors: Hao Guo, Wanxin Li, Mark Nejad, Chien-Chung Shen
works.title: Access Control for Electronic Health Records with Hybrid Blockchain-Edge Architecture
works.venue: Proc. 2019 IEEE Int. Conf. Blockchain (Blockchain), pp. 44-51, 2019
works.contribution: Proposes a hybrid architecture in which a blockchain-based controller manages identity and access control policies and serves as a tamper-proof log of access events, while off-chain edge nodes hold the EHR data and enforce attribute-based access control expressed in ALFA, working against the on-chain access control logs. Evaluated on Hyperledger Composer Fabric for smart-contract and ACL transaction processing time and response to unauthorized retrieval.
works.relevance: The most direct architectural precedent for SEBA-XAI's split: the authorisation decision is computed off-chain and the ledger holds policy plus a tamper-proof log. The gap this work leaves open is exactly the one SEBA-XAI targets. The on-chain log records that an access event happened, but nothing cryptographically binds the logged entry to the off-chain component that produced it, so a compromised or silently-swapped edge enforcer cannot be detected. SEBA-XAI adds an Ed25519 attestation checked against a ledger-registered adapter digest, a hash of the attributes the decider consumed, and a hash of the query, and it re-executes a deterministic engine on every endorsing peer rather than trusting the off-chain result unconditionally.

works.fullAuthors: Keke Gai, Yufeng She, Liehuang Zhu, Kim-Kwang Raymond Choo, Zhiguo Wan
works.title: A Blockchain-Based Access Control Scheme for Zero Trust Cross-Organizational Data Sharing
works.venue: ACM Transactions on Internet Technology, vol. 23, no. 3, pp. 1-25, Aug. 2023
works.contribution: Argues that contemporary access control schemes protect a single objective rather than multiple parties, and proposes a consortium-blockchain scheme for lightweight data sharing between mutually distrusting organizations. A Role-Based Access Control model is deployed via a proposed multi-signature protocol and smart contract methods; evaluated on Hyperledger Fabric with Caliper and BFT-SMaRT benchmarks.
works.relevance: The strongest ACM-venue treatment of the multi-organisation, zero-trust setting that SEBA-XAI's six-organisation police/forensics/prosecution/court network instantiates, and it shares the insight that a decision touching several parties should carry more than one signature. The difference is what the signatures attest: Gai et al. use multi-signature to gather organisational consent to an RBAC role assignment, whereas SEBA-XAI's two signatures come from structurally different parties, the requesting agency and an AI organisation holding its own MSP and peer, so the request and the decision are separable transactions with separable accountability. The decision function is also RBAC over roles, not attribute reasoning over a natural-language request, and produces no explanation artifact.

works.fullAuthors: Damiano Di Francesco Maesa, Paolo Mori, Laura Ricci
works.title: A blockchain based approach for the definition of auditable Access Control systems
works.venue: Computers & Security, vol. 84, pp. 93-119, Jul. 2019
works.contribution: Codifies attribute-based access control policies as smart contracts deployed on a blockchain, turning policy evaluation into fully distributed smart-contract execution; the attributes required for evaluation are likewise managed by on-chain contracts. Auditability follows from ledger immutability and transparency. Reference implementation translates XACML policies into Solidity contracts on Ethereum, including the case where the protected resources are themselves smart contracts, with experimental performance results and a discussion of drawbacks.
works.relevance: The reference work for auditable policy evaluation, and the source of the property SEBA-XAI must preserve while moving the hard part of the decision off-chain. Maesa et al. get auditability for free because evaluation is on-chain and deterministic; once a fine-tuned model produces the decision, that guarantee has to be reconstructed. SEBA-XAI does so by committing an attestation, an attribute-set hash and a query hash alongside a reason code, decisive attributes and a counterfactual, so an auditor can replay what the decider was shown. It is also the natural citation for the observation that on-chain XACML evaluation cannot express the open-textured, discretionary judgements that inter-agency case-record requests involve, which is why an ESCALATE outcome exists at all.

works.fullAuthors: Arnab Mukherjee, Raju Halder
works.title: PoliceChain: Blockchain-Based Smart Policing System for Smart Cities
works.venue: Proc. 13th Int. Conf. on Security of Information and Networks (SIN '20), ACM, pp. 1-5, 2020
works.contribution: Proposes a blockchain-based smart policing system for accountable storage, safeguarding and sharing of evidence and intelligence across investigations, criminal cases and justice information. Stakeholders include citizens, law enforcement, intelligence agencies, forensic departments, government bodies and judges, supporting FIR filing, investigation initiation, forensic report addition and delivery of justice. Proof of concept on Hyperledger Fabric using an Attribute-Based Access Control policy, with experimental evaluation. Claimed as the first blockchain-based smart policing proposal.
works.relevance: The closest domain precedent: a permissioned Fabric ledger with essentially SEBA-XAI's cast of organisations (police, forensics, judiciary) and ABAC over criminal case records. It establishes the application setting but stops at static attribute rules encoded in chaincode. There is no learned policy model, no natural-language access request, no ALLOW/DENY/ESCALATE tri-state with a human adjudication path, and no explanation committed as an audit artifact. It also has no AI organisation in the membership structure, so it cannot exhibit the two-party request/decision separation that SEBA-XAI claims as its novelty.

works.fullAuthors: Mahbubur Rahman, Liang Chen, Jonathan Loo, Wei Jie
works.title: Towards Deep Learning Based Access Control using Hyperledger-Fabric Blockchain for the Internet of Things
works.venue: Proc. 2023 IEEE 6th Int. Conf. on Cloud Computing and Artificial Intelligence: Technologies and Applications (CloudTech), pp. 1-8, 2023
works.contribution: Argues that existing blockchain-based access control approaches manage permissions but do not detect malicious anomalies, and proposes a deep-learning-based authorisation solution deployed within the Hyperledger Fabric private blockchain. Smart contracts define attribute-based access control policies augmented with an Artificial Neural Network model intended to identify and isolate malicious anomalies and block unauthorised access from malicious devices. Evaluated for security and performance.
works.relevance: The nearest prior work combining a learned model with Fabric-based ABAC, and therefore the sharpest point of comparison. It differs on every axis SEBA-XAI's contribution turns on: the learned component is a small ANN anomaly detector over device features rather than a fine-tuned LLM reasoning over a natural-language request; the model is folded into the chaincode rather than operated by a distinct MSP organisation, so there is no adapter digest to register, no attestation to verify and no second signing party; there is no deterministic engine holding override authority over the model; there is no escalation-to-human outcome; and the decision carries no reason code, decisive attributes or counterfactual. It also targets IoT device authorisation, not inter-agency criminal case records.
